Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions, and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [15, 34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. The study *Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers* tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy [1]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

Broader investigations into attention mechanisms and architectures provide context for these modifications. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to reduce attention to unneeded elements [8]. *Beyond Self-Attention: External Attention Using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks* proposes external attention for visual tasks [33]. *Depth-Attention: Cross-Layer Value Mixing for Language Models* observes that recent cross-layer methods operate on hidden states outside the standard attention flow [37]. Surveys such as *A Survey on Vision Transformer*, *Transformers in Vision: A Survey*, and *A survey of transformers* document the application of Transformers across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41]. *An Empirical Study of Spatial Attention Mechanisms in Deep Networks* examines how different influencing factors affect attention performance [28].

This study positions itself against these themes by isolating the effect of cross-layer query weight consistency from other regularization forms. While [17] and [18] suggest consistency aids domain adaptation and overfitting, [3] reports inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a similar setting. The disagreement between works proposing cross-layer mechanisms [15, 34] and those questioning transformer efficacy [5] motivates our boundary test. We do not claim attention stability from accuracy contrasts alone, nor do we generalize beyond the subject-disjoint setting defined in the preregistration.

=== method ===
The method centers on the CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator, which enforces Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block 0 and block 1 query projection weights. The hypothesis posits that stabilizing attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight during loss computation of every optimization step. The operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it.

The operator retrieves reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detaches them from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. It computes the element-wise difference between the target weights and the reference weights, squares these differences, and sums them over all elements to compute the raw loss. This raw loss is scaled by a fixed consistency_coefficient of 0.01 to prevent the loss_term from dominating the classification objective. The resulting loss_term is stored for harness aggregation and returned for addition to the training objective. Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients, ensuring the loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds.

The baseline condition serves as the comparator. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation.

The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with same shape and norm as block 0's weights, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This condition tests whether any observed effect arises from the regularization term itself or the specific cross-layer relationship. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method isolates the effect of the consistency loss from implementation variance by ensuring the only difference between the proposed condition and the baseline is the presence of the loss term.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to answer the question of generalization to unseen subjects, which a random split would not. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. This distinction is critical because generalization across subjects with different movement styles and sensor characteristics is the primary challenge in this domain. A random split would allow information leakage between training and testing sets via subject identity, inflating accuracy estimates and failing to test the robustness of the architectural bias.

**Pairing and Controls.** Pairing conditions by seed reduces variance attributable to initialization and data ordering, allowing for a more precise estimate of the intervention's effect. Each negative control's intended alternative explanation is that compute matching or regularization magnitude, rather than cross-layer consistency, drives any observed change. The observed contrast supports distinguishing meaningful structural regularization from arbitrary penalty terms. The seed budget of 43 primary and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds provides sufficient power to detect effects exceeding the registered margin, distinguishing zero-null detection from exceeding the margin. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin.

**Analysis Plan.** The analysis distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations. Here, replication is on new seeds within the same dataset and architecture, confirming stability across sampling variation. We report both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated. A calibration-noise threshold is not an independently justified threshold of scientific or practical importance, but the registered margin provides a consistent decision rule. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0007734 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). There was no statistically significant difference, as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 1 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition (0.9062), the baseline (0.9054), and the first negative control (0.9051). Figure 2 visualizes these means with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions, showing the paired mean difference over 43 seeds with the registered worthwhile threshold marked. The lower confidence bound does not exceed the threshold.

**Replication Cohort.** In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001957 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). There was no statistically significant difference, as the 95% CI includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Table 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition (0.9055), the baseline (0.9035), and the first negative control (0.9043). Figure 5 visualizes these means for the replication cohort. Figure 6 plots the mean difference, showing the paired mean difference over 43 seeds. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold; support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it, which it does not.

**Training Dynamics.** Figure 4 and Figure 7 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves for the conditions coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern. No value is jittered. The training dynamics do not suggest divergence in convergence behavior between the proposed condition and the baseline. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive regarding the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency improves accuracy.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. Both the primary and replication cohorts produced inconclusive results, with confidence intervals including zero and failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class, allowing deeper layers to refine features differently than shallower layers. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency coefficient was too small to influence learning, or that the Frobenius norm penalty does not align with the relevant feature space for subject-disjoint generalization. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment, and we do not claim attention stability from an accuracy contrast alone. The negative control confirms that the compute cost of the penalty term itself does not drive performance changes, as its accuracy was comparable to the baseline.

**Replication Value.** The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not due to a specific seed configuration. The replication cohort mean difference (0.001957) was slightly larger than the primary (0.0007734), but both remained within noise relative to the margin. This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is below the threshold of practical importance defined in the preregistration.

**Relation to Cited Work.** These findings agree with [3], which reported inconclusive results for spectral entropy minimization in a similar setting. They conflict with the hypothesis that consistency regularization universally improves generalization as suggested by [17], though [17] focused on machine translation tasks. They are not comparable to [18] in terms of intervention, task, data regime or evaluation, as [18] addressed domain adaptive semantic segmentation. The results support the view that transformers face limitations in time series prediction [32], and that architectural modifications require careful verification [5]. We do not rely on [2] due to its retracted status.

**Future Directions.** What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with deeper architectures or different regularization strengths. Future work should also measure attention maps directly to verify if stability is achieved even if accuracy does not improve.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency would work on different corpora, sensors, tasks, or deployment distributions. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects, but is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The study is limited to a 2-block transformer on the UCI HAR dataset; deeper models might exhibit different behavior regarding layer consistency. The registered margin reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. A null result here does not prove the mechanism is invalid, only that it did not exceed the margin under these conditions. Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism, which this study does not include.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin for held-out classification accuracy in either the primary or replication cohorts. The results are inconclusive, suggesting that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. For someone choosing between these methods, standard training remains preferable unless further evidence arises, as the intervention adds computational cost without demonstrated benefit. What would settle the question next is testing on deeper architectures and measuring attention stability directly. These findings indicate layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. Specific applications include biosignal data augmentation [20] and representing multivariate series as graphs [14], yet tackling time-series analysis usually involves designing separate models rather than using large pre-trained ones [22]. Furthermore, transformers face limitations in time series prediction, including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges [32]. This uncertainty motivates a rigorous test of specific architectural modifications intended to stabilize learning across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds.

A key open problem is determining what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects. One proposed mechanism is cross-layer consistency, where deeper layer weights are regularized toward shallower layer weights to stabilize attention patterns across depth. Various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms to address stability and generalization, noting that deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, motivating consistency constraints [18]. Cross-layer interactions are explored to strengthen layer interactions [15], and cross-layer consistency is applied to activation engineering [34]. However, there is a lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization. This work addresses this gap by testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling.

Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. This paper reports a calibrated testbed experiment enforcing Frobenius norm consistency regularization between block query projection weights during training.

- We evaluate the proposed condition against a baseline and negative control on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using an official subject-disjoint split.

Cross-layer interactions are explored in *Cross-Layer Retrospective Retrieving via Layer Attention*, which devises a mechanism to strengthen layer interactions [15], and *Global Evolutionary Steering: Refining Activation Steering Control via Cross-Layer Consistency* applies cross-layer consistency to activation engineering [34]. *Cross-layer fusion enhanced transformer network for remote sensing scene classification* utilizes cross-layer fusion to capture multi-scale features [23]. *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances accuracy [3]. Conversely, *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it [2].

While prior work establishes that consistency regularization can mitigate overfitting [17] and domain gaps affect attention [18], the specific effect of query projection alignment on subject-disjoint generalization remains unsettled. === method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Training proceeds for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD (learning rate 0.05, momentum 0.9).

The hypothesis is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. The intervention adds a loss term computed as the squared element-wise difference between the query projection weights of block 0 and block 1, scaled by a fixed coefficient. This regularization encourages deeper layer weights to remain close to shallower layer weights, testing whether attention stability across depth benefits generalization. The comparator neutralizes this effect by executing the identical code path but returning a zero loss term, ensuring that any difference in outcome is attributable to the regularization term rather than implementation artifacts.

The reference weights are retrieved from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight and detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only. The coefficient is fixed at 0.01 across all steps and seeds. This design ensures that the penalty influences the optimization of the deeper block's query projections without altering the earlier block's learning dynamics via backpropagation through the reference.

All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters. Evaluating on people who appear nowhere in training supports a claim about unseen subjects and is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution.

Attributing variation to the seeds that produced them allows us to quantify the stability of the effect across training runs rather than conflating it with subject variability. The seed budget supports the registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targeting rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin.

The negative control's intended alternative explanation is that any observed gain arises from the mere presence of an additional loss term or compute load rather than the specific cross-layer consistency. Its observed contrast supports whether the consistency relationship is necessary for any effect. The baseline ensures the harness is unbiased by verifying that the control arm records zero operator activity. The registered margin provides a consistent decision rule. A margin derived from calibration noise reflects measurement precision; it does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. We preserve the registered labels and report any exclusion of the target magnitude separately from its sign. The supplied power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; we do not claim the former guarantees the latter.

=== results ===
We walk through the evidence for the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts separately. Figure 1 shows the experimental flow, data ingestion, model architecture, registered conditions, the CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term, and subject-disjoint evaluation on the UCI HAR test split.

In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Table 2 reports the outcome for held-out classification accuracy in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.000773 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], paired randomisation p=0.657, Cohen's dz=0.06). The 95% CI includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Table 3 presents the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9055 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9090]), while the baseline achieved 0.9035 (95% CI [0.9000, 0.9070]). Figure 5 visualizes these means. Table 4 reports the outcome for held-out classification accuracy in the replication cohort. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00196 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], paired randomisation p=0.331, Cohen's dz=0.15). Figure 6 plots the paired mean difference. The 95% CI includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort.

Table 5 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for both cohorts. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered calibration-derived decision threshold.

This consistency across cohorts strengthens the conclusion that the effect, if any, is below the threshold of measurement precision defined in the preregistration.

This result suggests that cross-layer query consistency does not stabilize attention across depth in a way that improves subject-disjoint generalization for this architecture and task. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for transformers to accommodate different movement styles and sensor characteristics across subjects. The design does not establish whether cross-layer consistency would benefit larger models or different time-series domains. The margin reflects measurement precision, not practical importance, so we cannot claim the effect is practically negligible, only that it is undetectable given the calibration noise. What would settle the question next is testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks with larger architectures or different consistency targets, such as value or key projections.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency would benefit larger models or different time-series domains. The evaluation is limited to the UCI HAR dataset with 9 channels and 128-timestep windows; results may not generalize to different sensor modalities or sequence lengths. The margin reflects measurement precision, not practical importance, so we cannot claim the effect is practically negligible, only that it is undetectable given the calibration noise. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment. payload.content:
=== abstract ===

Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===

Time-series classification from wearable sensors enables continuous health monitoring, activity recognition, and human-computer interaction. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset represents a standard benchmark where inertial signals from smartphones must be classified into discrete activities across different subjects. Success in this setting requires models to generalize across individuals with different movement styles, sensor placements, and execution speeds—a subject-disjoint generalization challenge that remains difficult for deep architectures.

Transformers have attracted significant interest for time-series modeling due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms [38]. However, whether the architectural choices that make transformers effective in language and vision transfer to temporal domains remains contested. Some work questions whether transformers offer genuine advantages over simpler linear models for time-series forecasting [5], while others demonstrate successful applications in biosignal augmentation [20] and multivariate representation learning [14]. The uncertainty extends to architectural modifications: surveys document numerous transformer variants across domains [11, 21, 41], yet systematic evidence about which inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains limited.

One proposed mechanism for improving transformer generalization involves enforcing consistency across network depth. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17], and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention patterns [18]. Cross-layer mechanisms have been explored in various contexts: layer attention retrieves information from previous layers [15], cross-layer fusion captures multi-scale features [23], and cross-layer consistency has been applied to activation engineering [34]. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth could improve generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving the representational capacity needed for temporal feature learning.

**Gap and contribution.** This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Prior work has tested related regularization strategies—spectral entropy minimization of input projections [3] and entropy-maximized weight noise [2]—but cross-layer query consistency in time-series transformers has not undergone preregistered replication. The gap concerns whether this specific intervention, which penalizes divergence between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks, yields measurable accuracy improvements when evaluated on held-out subjects.

**What this paper does.** We report a preregistered experiment testing cross-layer query consistency regularization in a calibrated time-series transformer testbed. The study uses the official subject-disjoint split of UCI HAR, evaluates held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects, and includes both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters.

- We test whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, with a preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain.
- We report results from both primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 disjoint seeds) cohorts, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all estimates.
- We include a negative control that penalizes divergence from a fixed random matrix, isolating whether any observed effect stems from meaningful cross-layer relationships versus generic regularization.

**Preregistered prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. Transformers have achieved superior performances in natural language processing and computer vision, triggering interest in the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, the validity of this research line has been questioned: one study found that simple linear models outperformed sophisticated transformer-based forecasting models across nine real-life datasets, attributing this to temporal information loss from permutation-invariant self-attention [5]. This tension motivates careful evaluation of whether transformer architectural modifications genuinely improve time-series performance or merely add complexity without benefit.

Specific applications demonstrate transformers can work in temporal domains. Biosignal data augmentation using transformer-based conditional GANs has shown promise for expanding limited medical datasets [20]. Multivariate time series have been represented as graphs with attention mechanisms capturing both intra- and inter-series correlations [14]. Yet large pre-trained time-series models remain less common than in language and vision, with most tasks still requiring separate models designed from scratch [22]. Domain adaptation for time-series transformers faces limitations including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges under data shift [32]. These findings suggest that while transformers can process temporal data, their advantages over simpler architectures remain context-dependent.

**Consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies that constrain the solution space [17]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, leading to attention to spurious regions that deteriorate target domain accuracy [18]. Cross-layer interactions have been explored through mechanisms that strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from different receptive field levels [15]. Cross-layer consistency has also been applied to activation engineering, refining steering vectors through geometric stability across depth [34]. Cross-layer fusion has been utilized to capture multi-scale features in remote sensing classification [23]. These approaches share the hypothesis that coordinating representations across network depth improves generalization, though the specific mechanisms and target domains differ.

**Weight and spectral regularization.** Related work tests whether specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting but yielded inconclusive results: neither primary nor replication cohorts exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero [3]. This suggests that enforcing low-entropy singular value spectra on input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. Entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness carries a retracted notice because the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention [2]. These null and retracted findings underscore the importance of faithful implementation and preregistered replication when evaluating regularization hypotheses.

**Attention mechanism modifications.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms provide context for architectural modifications. Selective attention reduces attention to unneeded elements through a parameter-free change, improving language modeling performance across model sizes [8]. External attention using two linear layers offers linear complexity while implicitly considering correlations between samples [33]. Depth-attention performs cross-layer value mixing inside the attention module itself, adding no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache [37]. Surveys document transformer applications across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41], while empirical studies examine how different factors affect attention performance [28]. These works establish that attention mechanisms can be modified, but whether such modifications improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires direct testing.

**Positioning this study.** This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training [1]. Unlike cross-domain attention consistency which aligns attention maps across domains [18], or depth-attention which mixes values across layers [37], the intervention regularizes query projection weights between successive transformer blocks. The preregistered design with primary and confirmatory replication cohorts distinguishes this work from single-cohort evaluations. The subject-disjoint UCI HAR split tests generalization to unseen individuals rather than random held-out windows, addressing whether the intervention improves robustness to inter-subject variability in movement patterns and sensor characteristics.

=== method ===

**Operator design.** The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks. The target parameter is blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight with shape (64, 64). The reference parameter is blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight, detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The operator computes element-wise subtraction between target and reference weights, squares each element, sums over all elements, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective during every optimization step, so the combined objective is differentiated and the target parameters are trained by it.

**Why this expression.** The hypothesis is that stabilizing query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving representational capacity. Query projections determine which features each attention head attends to; if these projections diverge substantially across layers, deeper layers may learn idiosyncratic attention patterns that do not generalize to new subjects. Regularizing toward earlier layers tests whether consistent attention mechanisms across depth benefit temporal feature learning more than layer-specific adaptation. The Frobenius norm provides a differentiable measure of weight divergence that can be added to the training objective without modifying the architecture or inference path.

**Comparator and controls.** The baseline condition executes identical code but returns zero loss term, leaving the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This control arm reaches every registered lifecycle point on the same inputs, ensuring that any difference between conditions stems from the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, testing whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization.

**Gradient handling.** Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from the consistency loss. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, so block 1 query projections are trained toward block 0's current weights without modifying block 0 through this pathway. Block 0 still receives gradients from the classification objective through its own forward pass. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. Detaching the reference tensor stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient.

**Model architecture.** The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. Final LayerNorm(64) is followed by mean-pool over time and Linear(64,6) for classification. The 9 input channels correspond to the raw inertial signals from the UCI HAR dataset.

**Training and evaluation.** Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy as number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

**Operator specification.** CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step.
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective.

Algorithm 1: (1) Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight. (2) Detach reference_weights from gradient graph. (3) Compute diff = target - reference_weights. (4) Compute squared_elements = diff * diff. (5) Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements). (6) Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01. (7) Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw. (8) Store loss_term in scratch dict. (9) Return loss_term to harness.

=== experimental_setup ===

**Subject-disjoint split justification.** The official UCI HAR subject-disjoint split separates training and test subjects entirely, with 7,352 training windows from some subjects and 2,947 held-out windows from different subjects. This design answers whether the intervention improves generalization to unseen individuals rather than merely fitting the training distribution better. A random split would hold out windows from the same subjects used in training, conflating within-subject temporal generalization with between-subject generalization. For activity recognition applications where models must work for new users without subject-specific fine-tuning, the subject-disjoint evaluation is the relevant test. The cost is higher variance: inter-subject variability in movement style, sensor placement, and execution speed increases outcome noise compared to random splits.

The benefit is tighter confidence intervals for the paired difference; the cost is that seeds are not independent across conditions. The seed budget comprises 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The identities are recorded in the appendix.

**Negative control purpose.** The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix, destroying the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute. This tests whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization toward an arbitrary target. If the proposed condition outperforms the negative control, this would support the hypothesis that cross-layer consistency specifically (rather than any weight constraint) matters. If both perform similarly, the effect may stem from generic regularization rather than meaningful cross-layer relationships.

The analysis computed confidence intervals, not standard deviations. The registered normal-approximation sample-size calculation targets rejecting a zero-effect null at a true effect equal to the margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This does not give that power for the stricter support rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed the margin. === discussion ===

**Principal finding.** The cross-layer query consistency intervention did not yield statistically significant improvements in held-out classification accuracy in either the primary cohort (mean difference 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]) or the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds (mean difference 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Both confidence intervals include zero, and neither lower bound exceeds the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights across transformer blocks does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this calibrated testbed.

**Interpretation.** These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation remains essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. If cross-layer consistency improved generalization, we would expect the proposed condition to outperform the baseline with a confidence interval excluding zero and exceeding the worthwhile margin. Instead, the point estimates are small (0.000773 and 0.00196) and the intervals span both negative and positive values. One interpretation is that different transformer layers benefit from learning distinct query projections that capture different temporal features or abstraction levels. Regularizing toward earlier layers may constrain this layer-specific specialization without providing compensating benefits.

**Alternative mechanisms.** An alternative explanation is that the consistency penalty was too weak to produce measurable effects. The coefficient of 0.01 was chosen to prevent the loss term from dominating the classification objective, but this may have rendered the regularization ineffective. However, the negative control also used the same coefficient and showed similar performance to the proposed condition, suggesting the issue is not merely penalty strength but rather the nature of the constraint itself. Another alternative is that two transformer blocks are insufficient depth for cross-layer consistency to matter; deeper networks might show different behavior. This claim is untestable on this calibrated testbed, which pins one architecture at one size.

**What the replication cohort adds.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides confidence that the null result is not an artifact of a specific seed set. Both cohorts show the same pattern: small, nonsignificant differences with confidence intervals including zero. The replication cohort's effect size (dz=0.15) is larger than the primary (dz=0.06), but both remain far from the threshold needed to claim the intervention exceeds the worthwhile margin. This consistency across seed sets strengthens the conclusion that the intervention does not produce robust accuracy gains in this regime.

**Relation to cited work.** These findings align with prior null results on weight geometry regularization in subject-disjoint time-series settings. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections also yielded inconclusive results with confidence intervals including zero in both primary and replication cohorts [3]. This suggests a broader pattern: enforcing specific weight structures does not reliably improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The findings contrast with cross-domain attention consistency work that reported improvements in domain adaptive semantic segmentation [18], but that study addressed a different problem (domain shift across datasets rather than subject disjointness within a dataset) and used attention-map alignment rather than weight alignment. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Mechanistic hypotheses.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, not attention outputs or attention maps. Whether weight consistency translates to attention stability depends on how query projections interact with key and value projections during the attention computation, which was not measured. Future work could directly measure attention map similarity across layers to test whether weight regularization produces the hypothesized attention stabilization.

**Scope of generalization.** All claims are scoped to the calibrated testbed: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden channels, 4-head attention, on UCI HAR with official subject-disjoint split. The findings do not establish whether cross-layer consistency would help in larger models, different architectures, or other time-series datasets. A claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed. The single calibrated model at one size is what was tested; generalization to other settings requires separate experiments.

=== limitations ===

**Architecture and scale.** The study tests one architecture at one size: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks and 64 hidden channels. Whether cross-layer query consistency would benefit deeper transformers, different attention mechanisms, or larger hidden dimensions remains unknown. Claims about larger models are untestable on this calibrated testbed. The intervention may behave differently in architectures where depth plays a more substantial role in representation learning.

**Attention mechanism not measured.** The study does not measure attention maps directly. Claims about attention stability across layers are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, but whether this produces more stable or consistent attention patterns was not assessed. Direct measurement of attention maps would be needed to test the hypothesized mechanism.

**Dataset specificity.** Results are limited to the UCI HAR dataset with its specific sensor modality (smartphone inertial signals), activity classes (6 activities), and subject population. Whether the findings generalize to other time-series domains (physiological signals, financial data, environmental sensors) or other subject-disjoint benchmarks requires separate testing. The subject-disjoint split tests generalization to unseen individuals within this dataset, not to different corpora, sensors, or tasks.

**Coefficient and penalty strength.** The consistency coefficient of 0.01 was fixed across all conditions. Whether different coefficient values would produce different results was not tested. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient; the actual penalty magnitude depends on the weight divergence, which varies during training. The chosen value may have been too weak to produce measurable effects or too strong and interfered with task learning.

=== conclusion ===

This preregistered study tested whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary seeds and 43 pre-specified confirmatory replication seeds on disjoint seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between standard training and cross-layer query consistency regularization in this setting, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention. The findings suggest layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks in this architecture class. What would settle the question next: direct measurement of attention maps to test whether weight regularization produces attention stability, testing in deeper architectures where cross-layer effects might be more pronounced, and evaluation on additional subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks to assess whether the null result generalizes beyond UCI HAR.

=== abstract ===

Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.000773 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===

Time-series classification from wearable sensors enables continuous health monitoring, activity recognition, and human-computer interaction. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset represents a standard benchmark where inertial signals from smartphones must be classified into discrete activities across different subjects. Success in this setting requires models to generalize across individuals with different movement styles, sensor placements, and execution speeds—a subject-disjoint generalization challenge that remains difficult for deep architectures.

Transformers have attracted significant interest for time-series modeling due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms [38]. However, whether the architectural choices that make transformers effective in language and vision transfer to temporal domains remains contested. Some work questions whether transformers offer genuine advantages over simpler linear models for time-series forecasting [5], while others demonstrate successful applications in biosignal augmentation [20] and multivariate representation learning [14]. The uncertainty extends to architectural modifications: surveys document numerous transformer variants across domains [11, 21, 41], yet systematic evidence about which inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers remains limited.

One proposed mechanism for improving transformer generalization involves enforcing consistency across network depth. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data [17], and domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention patterns [18]. Cross-layer mechanisms have been explored in various contexts: layer attention retrieves information from previous layers [15], cross-layer fusion captures multi-scale features [23], and cross-layer consistency has been applied to activation engineering [34]. The hypothesis is that stabilizing attention patterns across depth could improve generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving the representational capacity needed for temporal feature learning.

**Gap and contribution.** This work addresses the lack of independent verification regarding whether cross-layer query consistency loss stabilizes attention across depth to improve subject-disjoint generalization, testing if the registered conclusion remains stable under fresh sampling. Prior work has tested related regularization strategies—spectral entropy minimization of input projections [3] and entropy-maximized weight noise [2]—but cross-layer query consistency in time-series transformers has not undergone preregistered replication. The gap concerns whether this specific intervention, which penalizes divergence between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks, yields measurable accuracy improvements when evaluated on held-out subjects.

**What this paper does.** We report a preregistered experiment testing cross-layer query consistency regularization in a calibrated time-series transformer testbed. The study uses the official subject-disjoint split of UCI HAR, evaluates held-out classification accuracy on 2,947 test windows from unseen subjects, and includes both a primary cohort and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. All conditions share paired seeds with identical initialization, data ordering, and hyperparameters.

- We test whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers, with a preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain.
- We report results from both primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 disjoint seeds) cohorts, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all estimates.
- We include a negative control that penalizes divergence from a fixed random matrix, isolating whether any observed effect stems from meaningful cross-layer relationships versus generic regularization.

**Preregistered prediction.** The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===

Research into Transformers for time-series analysis highlights both potential and uncertainty regarding their effectiveness and generalization. Transformers have achieved superior performances in natural language processing and computer vision, triggering interest in the time series community due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies [38]. However, the validity of this research line has been questioned: one study found that simple linear models outperformed sophisticated transformer-based forecasting models across nine real-life datasets, attributing this to temporal information loss from permutation-invariant self-attention [5]. This tension motivates careful evaluation of whether transformer architectural modifications genuinely improve time-series performance or merely add complexity without benefit.

Specific applications demonstrate transformers can work in temporal domains. Biosignal data augmentation using transformer-based conditional GANs has shown promise for expanding limited medical datasets [20]. Multivariate time series have been represented as graphs with attention mechanisms capturing both intra- and inter-series correlations [14]. Yet large pre-trained time-series models remain less common than in language and vision, with most tasks still requiring separate models designed from scratch [22]. Domain adaptation for time-series transformers faces limitations including insufficient temporal understanding and generalization challenges under data shift [32]. These findings suggest that while transformers can process temporal data, their advantages over simpler architectures remain context-dependent.

**Consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms.** To address stability and generalization, various works propose consistency regularization and cross-layer mechanisms. Deep transformer models are prone to overfitting on small-scale training data, motivating regularization strategies that constrain the solution space [17]. Domain gaps can cause discrepancies in self-attention, leading to attention to spurious regions that deteriorate target domain accuracy [18]. Cross-layer interactions have been explored through mechanisms that strengthen layer interactions by retrieving query-related information from different receptive field levels [15]. Cross-layer consistency has also been applied to activation engineering, refining steering vectors through geometric stability across depth [34]. Cross-layer fusion has been utilized to capture multi-scale features in remote sensing classification [23]. These approaches share the hypothesis that coordinating representations across network depth improves generalization, though the specific mechanisms and target domains differ.

**Weight and spectral regularization.** Related work tests whether specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting but yielded inconclusive results: neither primary nor replication cohorts exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero [3]. This suggests that enforcing low-entropy singular value spectra on input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. Entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness carries a retracted notice because the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention [2]. These null and retracted findings underscore the importance of faithful implementation and preregistered replication when evaluating regularization hypotheses.

**Attention mechanism modifications.** Broader investigations into attention mechanisms provide context for architectural modifications. Selective attention reduces attention to unneeded elements through a parameter-free change, improving language modeling performance across model sizes [8]. External attention using two linear layers offers linear complexity while implicitly considering correlations between samples [33]. Depth-attention performs cross-layer value mixing inside the attention module itself, adding no persistent inference state beyond the standard key-value cache [37]. Surveys document transformer applications across vision, NLP, and audio [11, 21, 41], while empirical studies examine how different factors affect attention performance [28]. These works establish that attention mechanisms can be modified, but whether such modifications improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers requires direct testing.

**Positioning this study.** This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training [1]. Unlike cross-domain attention consistency which aligns attention maps across domains [18], or depth-attention which mixes values across layers [37], the intervention regularizes query projection weights between successive transformer blocks. The preregistered design with primary and confirmatory replication cohorts distinguishes this work from single-cohort evaluations. The subject-disjoint UCI HAR split tests generalization to unseen individuals rather than random held-out windows, addressing whether the intervention improves robustness to inter-subject variability in movement patterns and sensor characteristics.

=== method ===

**Operator design.** The CrossLayerQueryConsistency operator enforces Frobenius norm consistency between query projection weights in successive transformer blocks. The target parameter is blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight with shape (64, 64). The reference parameter is blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight, detached from the gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0. The operator computes element-wise subtraction between target and reference weights, squares each element, sums over all elements, and scales by a fixed coefficient of 0.01. This loss term is added to the classification objective during every optimization step, so the combined objective is differentiated and the target parameters are trained by it.

**Why this expression.** The hypothesis is that stabilizing query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization by reducing layer-specific overfitting while preserving representational capacity. Query projections determine which features each attention head attends to; if these projections diverge substantially across layers, deeper layers may learn idiosyncratic attention patterns that do not generalize to new subjects. Regularizing toward earlier layers tests whether consistent attention mechanisms across depth benefit temporal feature learning more than layer-specific adaptation. The Frobenius norm provides a differentiable measure of weight divergence that can be added to the training objective without modifying the architecture or inference path.

**Comparator and controls.** The baseline condition executes identical code but returns zero loss term, leaving the registered target parameter and optimizer momentum buffer unchanged. This control arm reaches every registered lifecycle point on the same inputs, ensuring that any difference between conditions stems from the loss term itself rather than implementation artifacts. The first negative control penalizes difference between block 1 weights and a fixed random matrix with the same shape and norm as block 0's weights. This destroys the meaningful cross-layer relationship while matching compute, testing whether any observed effect requires alignment between actual layer weights versus generic weight regularization.

**Gradient handling.** Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients from the consistency loss. The loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only, so block 1 query projections are trained toward block 0's current weights without modifying block 0 through this pathway. Block 0 still receives gradients from the classification objective through its own forward pass. The coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds. Detaching the reference tensor stops that penalty's gradient only; it does not freeze the tensor's task-loss gradient.

**Model architecture.** The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear projection (9 to 64 channels), a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 channels), and two transformer blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. Final LayerNorm(64) is followed by mean-pool over time and Linear(64,6) for classification. The 9 input channels correspond to the raw inertial signals from the UCI HAR dataset.

**Training and evaluation.** Training runs for 12 epochs with batch size 128, SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Evaluation measures held-out classification accuracy as number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them.

**Operator specification.** CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step.
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents loss_term from dominating classification objective.

Algorithm 1: (1) Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight. (2) Detach reference_weights from gradient graph. (3) Compute diff = target - reference_weights. (4) Compute squared_elements = diff * diff. (5) Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements). (6) Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01. (7) Compute loss_term = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw. (8) Store loss_term in scratch dict. (9) Return loss_term to harness.

This suggests a broader pattern: enforcing specific weight structures does not reliably improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The findings contrast with cross-domain attention consistency work that reported improvements in domain adaptive semantic segmentation [18], but that study addressed a different problem (domain shift across datasets rather than subject disjointness within a dataset) and used attention-map alignment rather than weight alignment. Weight alignment is not attention-map alignment.

**Mechanistic hypotheses.** Mechanistic rationales are hypotheses unless the supplied results contain direct measurements of that mechanism. The study does not measure attention maps directly, so claims about attention stability are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, not attention outputs or attention maps. Whether weight consistency translates to attention stability depends on how query projections interact with key and value projections during the attention computation, which was not measured. Future work could directly measure attention map similarity across layers to test whether weight regularization produces the hypothesized attention stabilization.

**Scope of generalization.** All claims are scoped to the calibrated testbed: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 64 hidden channels, 4-head attention, on UCI HAR with official subject-disjoint split. The findings do not establish whether cross-layer consistency would help in larger models, different architectures, or other time-series datasets. A claim about model scale or architecture family is untestable on this calibrated testbed. The single calibrated model at one size is what was tested; generalization to other settings requires separate experiments.

=== limitations ===

**Architecture and scale.** The study tests one architecture at one size: PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks and 64 hidden channels. Whether cross-layer query consistency would benefit deeper transformers, different attention mechanisms, or larger hidden dimensions remains unknown. Claims about larger models are untestable on this calibrated testbed. The intervention may behave differently in architectures where depth plays a more substantial role in representation learning.

**Attention mechanism not measured.** The study does not measure attention maps directly. Claims about attention stability across layers are mechanistic hypotheses rather than measured findings. The intervention regularizes query projection weights, but whether this produces more stable or consistent attention patterns was not assessed. Direct measurement of attention maps would be needed to test the hypothesized mechanism.

**Dataset specificity.** Results are limited to the UCI HAR dataset with its specific sensor modality (smartphone inertial signals), activity classes (6 activities), and subject population. Whether the findings generalize to other time-series domains (physiological signals, financial data, environmental sensors) or other subject-disjoint benchmarks requires separate testing. The subject-disjoint split tests generalization to unseen individuals within this dataset, not to different corpora, sensors, or tasks.

**Coefficient and penalty strength.** The consistency coefficient of 0.01 was fixed across all conditions. Whether different coefficient values would produce different results was not tested. A small coefficient alone does not guarantee a small penalty or gradient; the actual penalty magnitude depends on the weight divergence, which varies during training. The chosen value may have been too weak to produce measurable effects or too strong and interfered with task learning.

=== conclusion ===

This preregistered study tested whether cross-layer query consistency regularization improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Across 43 primary seeds and 43 pre-specified confirmatory replication seeds on disjoint seeds, the intervention produced small, statistically nonsignificant accuracy differences (primary: 0.000773, 95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436]; replication: 0.00196, 95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571]). Neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. For someone choosing between standard training and cross-layer query consistency regularization in this setting, the evidence does not support adopting the intervention. The findings suggest layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks in this architecture class. What would settle the question next: direct measurement of attention maps to test whether weight regularization produces attention stability, testing in deeper architectures where cross-layer effects might be more pronounced, and evaluation on additional subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks to assess whether the null result generalizes beyond UCI HAR.

=== appendix ===

**Seed identities.** The 43 primary seed identities and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seed identities are recorded in the experiment archive but not enumerated in the prose per registration requirements.

**Figure descriptions.** Figure 1: Methodology flow showing UCI HAR data processing through PreNormTransformerEncoder with CrossLayerQueryConsistency intervention at the loss term across registered conditions, evaluated on the official test split for classification accuracy. Figure 2: Mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 3: Mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 4: Mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the primary cohort. Figure 5: Mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6: Mean difference between proposed and baseline in the replication cohort. Figure 7: Mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for all conditions in the replication cohort.

**Data availability.** UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K).
